subjects.introduction: Steadfastness is easy to profess and hard to recognise. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá makes it recognisable in unexpected places: in a tree that bears fruit only because its roots hold, in a vineyard that lives on no other water, in the refusal to backbite, in the patience owed to a friend who is uncertain. He teaches that no power but the Covenant can keep a community one, and that firmness in it is measured not by the fierceness of a person’s loyalty but by a readiness to give one’s life for the friends of God. The covenant set before Israel in Deuteronomy places the choice between life and death near enough to act on [1]; Jesus binds abiding in his love to keeping his commandments [2]; the Qur’an warns that a pledge can be unravelled by the way one treats others [3]. From here the path leads to the ark that shelters those who board it, to the Covenant’s work in preserving unity, and to the prayers that ask for a firmness no one can supply alone.
